Bug Title: Long-lived API secret stored in localStorage
Steps to Reproduce:
1. Account: sign in as OC — kak713.oc@lighthouseconnect.org / Kak@123 (any account works).
2. Press F12 -> click the Application tab (Chrome) or Storage tab (Firefox).
3. In the left panel expand Local Storage -> click the uat.lighthouseconnect.org entry.
4. In the table, find the keys api_key and api_secret — their values are shown in plain text.
5. Point out: this is the account's API credential, sitting in localStorage where any script on the page (or a browser extension) can read it, and it stays valid for seven days.
Expected Result: The protective setting is in place and the unsafe request is refused.
Actual Result: login stores Frappe api_key/api_secret in localStorage; every request sends Authorization: token <key>:<secret>.
Suggested Fix: move the session to a short-lived, httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie so it cannot be read from JavaScript, and shorten its lifetime. A token in localStorage is readable by any script on the origin — and the persona applications share a single origin, so an XSS in any one of them yields a credential valid for the others.

Bug Title: 14 routes render blank on direct load
Persona / Role: Facilitator and Counsellor, Skilling Partner, Skilling Youth Coordinator
Steps to Reproduce:
1. Account: sign in as FC — kak713.fc@lighthouseconnect.org / Kak@123.
2. In the address bar, type the URL directly: uat.lighthouseconnect.org/fc/badge-table (do not click to it from the menu — type or paste it).
3. Press Enter. The page loads blank — header/sidebar only, no content.
4. Press F12 to open developer tools, click the Console tab.
5. Read the red error: "Cannot read properties of null (reading 'viewType')".
6. Now reach the same screen by clicking through the app's menu instead — it renders. The bug is that the screen only works when opened from inside the app, not by direct URL, refresh, or bookmark.
7. Repeat for /fc/view-post-test and /fc/batch-management/view-batch to show it is not a one-off.
Expected Result: The screen renders its content when the URL is opened directly, refreshed, or reached from a bookmark.
Actual Result: the full suite executed three consecutive times. Each route below rendered nothing in every execution, so environmental flake is excluded — routes failing in only some executions are classified separately and are not listed here. Body renders 0 characters.
Suggested Fix: root-caused separately to a null navigation state. These routes read their identifier from React Router state, which is absent on a direct load or a refresh. Read the identifier from URL parameters and guard the read. One fix closes this and the group-based route failures below.

Bug Title: Systematic WCAG critical violations, concentrated in shared navigation
Steps to Reproduce:
1. Account: sign in as any persona (OC).
2. On any screen, right-click the left-hand navigation sidebar -> Inspect.
3. In the Elements panel, observe the list markup: <li> items that are not wrapped in a <ul>, and navigation images with no alt attribute.
4. A screen-reader user cannot identify these navigation items. This markup is in the shared sidebar, so it is wrong on every page of every persona app.
5. For the full list, run axe DevTools (browser extension) on any page, or see our recorded axe-core results.
Actual Result: The distribution matters as much as the count. Four rules fire on every route scanned, in every persona. This is not 23 pages each carrying its own mistakes. It is one shared layout and navigation component, repeated across all of them. The 181 orphaned <li> elements and the unlabelled icon images match the sidebar navigation observed during route mapping. Impact: a screen-reader user cannot identify navigation items (no alt text), cannot operate icon-only buttons (no accessible name), and meets a malformed list structure on every page.
Suggested Fix: correct the sidebar list markup (<li> inside <ul>), add alt to nav icons, give icon-only buttons an aria-label, and remove ARIA attributes not permitted on their roles — all in the shared navigation component.

Bug Title: The frontend is served with no security headers at all
Steps to Reproduce:
1. Account: none needed — do this on the login page.
2. Open uat.lighthouseconnect.org, press F12 -> Network tab, then reload the page.
3. In the Network list click the very first request (the document / the app URL itself).
4. Open the Response Headers section on the right.
5. Point out what is ABSENT: no Content-Security-Policy, no X-Frame-Options, no X-Content-Type-Options, no Strict-Transport-Security, no Referrer-Policy.
6. Fastest confirmation for the record: run node verify/run.mjs --only WC-112 which checks all five headers at once.
Expected Result: The protective setting is in place and the unsafe request is refused.
Actual Result: HEAD https://uat.lighthouseconnect.org/ returns, in full: Server: nginx/1.24.0 (Ubuntu), Date, Content-Type, Content-Length, Connection, Last-Modified, ETag, Accept-Ranges. None of the following is present:; Header; Absent; What it would prevent; Content-Security-Policy; yes; Cross-site scripting, and exfiltration of anything readable from the page; Strict-Transport-Security; yes; Protocol downgrade … (full detail in the findings register)
Suggested Fix: add the headers at the nginx layer serving the frontend. A reasonable starting set is Strict-Transport-Security with a long max-age, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, X-Frame-Options: DENY (or a CSP frame-ancestors directive), and a Content-Security-Policy developed in report-only mode first so it can be tuned without breaking the applications. Moving the session off localStorage and onto the httpOnly cookie the API already issues would remove the underlying exposure.

Bug Title: Committed env files in frontend repos
Steps to Reproduce:
1. Shown in the repository.
2. Open any frontend repo and confirm .env, .env.uat and .env.prod are committed (they appear in the file list and in git history).
3. Environment configuration should be supplied at build time, not committed to source.
Expected Result: Everything needed to build and run the platform is present in the repositories the foundation owns.
Actual Result: hygiene; .env.prod should not be committed. (Contents not inspected.)
Suggested Fix: supply environment configuration at build time (CI variables or an untracked .env.local), keep only a committed .env.example, and add .env* to .gitignore with the example excepted. This also removes the possibility of a credential being added to one of these files later and inherited by every fork and clone.

Bug Title: Forgot Password link is a dead anchor
Steps to Reproduce:
1. Account: none — the login page.
2. Open the login screen and click the 'Forgot Password' link.
3. Observe: nothing happens — the link does not navigate. Right-click it -> Inspect and confirm the anchor points at href="#" rather than the reset route.
4. Effect: a user who forgets their password has no working way to reset it from the UI.
Expected Result: The screen renders its content when the URL is opened directly, refreshed, or reached from a bookmark.
Suggested Fix: point the anchor at the password-reset route, or remove it until that route exists. The backend already exposes authentication.api.password.send_otp / verify_otp / reset_password, so the flow exists server-side and only the entry point is missing. A user who forgets their password currently has no self-service path at all.

Bug Title: Colour contrast below WCAG AA on 13 routes
Steps to Reproduce:
1. Account: sign in as any persona (OC).
2. Open any dashboard. Right-click a faint label or secondary button -> Inspect.
3. In DevTools, the Accessibility / Contrast indicator shows the text/background ratio below the WCAG AA threshold of 4.5:1.
4. This was measured across 13 routes; the failures sit in shared components so they recur widely.
Suggested Fix: the failures are concentrated in shared navigation and shared button styles rather than spread across pages, so correcting the palette tokens in the shared component library (persona-common-components) fixes most instances at once. Target WCAG AA — 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text and UI boundaries — and add an automated contrast check to CI so regressions are caught at build time.

Bug Title: Frontend dependencies carry known high-severity advisories, including the HTTP client used by every application
Steps to Reproduce:
1. Shown by running one command per app.
2. In any frontend repo run: npm audit --audit-level=high
3. Read the summary. Across the nine JS projects there are 14 critical and 181 high advisories; the four criticals are test tooling, but axios — the HTTP client used for every API call — is affected in 8 of 9 apps.
Expected Result: Build and release hygiene: no development artefacts, warnings or broken copy in a deployed application.
Actual Result: npm audit across the nine committed lockfiles reports 14 critical, 181 high, 74 moderate, 9 low. Separating runtime from build dependencies: 8 distinct critical/high packages reach users, 26 do not. All four criticals are test tooling (vitest, tinypool, @vitest/coverage-v8, a form-data path beneath them). axios, the HTTP client used to call the backend, is affected in 8 of 9 projects; the react-router family in 5.
Suggested Fix: Run npm audit fix in each project and commit the updated lockfile. Start with axios: highest value, lowest risk. Treat any react-router major upgrade as separate work, since it interacts with WC-043. Add npm audit --audit-level=high to CI, which currently has no dependency check.

Bug Title: Two live Google API keys are committed to the repositories, one hardcoded in a source file
Steps to Reproduce:
1. Shown in source.
2. Open weconnect-frontend/.env (and .env.uat, .env.prod): VITE_MAP_API_KEY holds a live Google key in plain text.
3. Open weconnect-frontend-fc/src/components/google-map/google-map.jsx: a second key is hardcoded directly in the source.
4. Both are in git history, so they must be rotated, not just deleted.
Expected Result: No API key is committed; keys live in the build environment and are restricted by HTTP referrer.
Actual Result: Two keys committed. Tested with one Geocoding request each and no referrer: the first returns REQUEST_DENIED "You must enable Billing" (cannot be charged); the second returns REQUEST_DENIED "This API is not activated". Neither is currently usable, which is why this is S3.
Suggested Fix: Rotate both keys in the Google Cloud console (deleting the lines does not help — they are in git history). Move the replacement into the build environment, restrict by HTTP referrer to the foundation's hosts, and remove the hardcoded key from google-map.jsx.

Bug Title: Backend-supplied content is rendered as raw HTML, giving a stored cross-site scripting path
Steps to Reproduce:
1. This is shown in the source, not the running app (demonstrating it live could execute injected HTML).
2. Open the repo file: weconnect-frontend/src/pages/outreach-planning/outreach-community/target-card.jsx, line 147.
3. Point to: dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: strategy }} — this renders backend-supplied text as raw HTML, bypassing React's escaping.
4. The open question for the client: who can edit the 'recommended strategy' text? If any user can, a script stored there runs for everyone who opens the community dashboard.
Expected Result: User-supplied content is escaped or sanitised before rendering; raw HTML is not injected.
Actual Result: One dangerouslySetInnerHTML across the entire frontend estate, at target-card.jsx:147, rendering the backend-supplied 'strategy' string as raw HTML. Whether the field is user-writable is not yet confirmed.
Suggested Fix: If the field only needs bold or line breaks, render as text and format in the component. If HTML must be supported, sanitise on input with an allowlist (DOMPurify). First answer: who can edit the recommended strategy text?

Bug Title: Source-tree asset path in built app
Steps to Reproduce:
1. Shown in the deployed build output, not the running UI.
2. Open the browser on any persona app, press F12 -> Sources (or Debugger) tab.
3. Search the loaded bundle for a source-tree path such as '/src/' that leaked into the shipped asset reference.
4. Confirm the built app references a development path rather than the built asset path.
Expected Result: Build and release hygiene: no development artefacts, warnings or broken copy in a deployed application.
Suggested Fix: import the asset so the bundler fingerprints and rewrites its path, rather than referencing /src/... literally. As shipped the path only resolves by accident of how the site is served, and will 404 under any stricter static configuration.

Steps to Reproduce:
1. Account: sign in as any persona (OC).
2. Open any screen, press F12 -> Console tab.
3. On page load, read the React Router v6 'future flag' warnings printed to the console.

Steps to Reproduce:
1. Shown in the frontend source.
2. Open the affected app's src/routes.js (or App.jsx).
3. Find the route defined with a doubled path segment (e.g. a path that resolves to /fc/fc/...).
4. Correct the duplicated segment so the route resolves once.
Expected Result: Build and release hygiene: no development artefacts, warnings or broken copy in a deployed application.
Actual Result: FC nav links use /fc/fc/all-batches, /fc/fc/counselling, /fc/fc/tasks (double fc). Works, but smells like a base-path bug.

Make the links relative to the router base, or drop the base from the basename configuration — one or the other, not both. It works today only because the server tolerates the duplicated segment.

Steps to Reproduce:
1. Account: sign in as any persona.
2. Right-click a navigation item that does nothing when clicked -> Inspect.
3. Confirm the anchor is <a href="#"> — a placeholder link that was never wired to a destination.
Expected Result: The screen renders its content when the URL is opened directly, refreshed, or reached from a bookmark.
Actual Result: 10 across the sampled routes — CH 6, FC 3, and "Forgot Password?" on the shared login page. They render as links, respond to hover, and do nothing when clicked.
Suggested Fix: give each anchor a real destination, or use a <button> where the element triggers an action rather than navigation. An href="#" is announced to assistive technology as a link that goes nowhere, and it scrolls the page to the top when activated — so this is an accessibility defect as well as a cosmetic one.
